etymology: Superlative of utter (Old English ūtera, outer), from ūt, out. Webster 1828: extreme; being in the furthest, greatest or highest degree. The Authorized Version uses it two ways — of distance, the uttermost part of the earth, and of degree, saved to the uttermost. The second is where the gospel lives.
biblical_def: Uttermost is the Authorized Version’s word for the far edge — of the map, or of the case. Geographically it marks the end of the known world: Ask of me, and I shall give thee the heathen for thine inheritance, and the uttermost parts of the earth for thy possession (Psalm 2:8), and the risen Christ sends His witnesses unto the uttermost part of the earth (Acts 1:8). Morally it marks the limit of endurance under wrath: the wrath is come upon them to the uttermost (1 Thessalonians 2:16). But the word’s whole weight rests on one verse: Wherefore he is able also to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him, seeing he ever liveth to make intercession for them (Hebrews 7:25). The Greek there is pantelēs — completely, to the very end, with nothing left over. It answers the question every awakened conscience actually asks. Not can He save? but can He save all the way, and keep saving? The clause that follows supplies the ground: He ever liveth. The salvation is uttermost because the Priest is undying. This is the confessional doctrine of perseverance compressed into one adverb. Christ does not save a man to a point and then hand him back to himself. He saves to the uttermost, because His intercession never lapses and the Father never refuses the Son.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines UTTERMOST as extreme; being in the furthest, greatest or highest degree. As a noun it is the greatest, the utmost extent. Webster marks it the superlative of utter and interchangeable with utmost.
webster_full: UTTERMOST, a. [utter and most.] — Extreme; being in the furthest, greatest or highest degree; as the uttermost extent or end. UTTERMOST, n. — The greatest; the utmost extent or degree.
Webster keeps the word quantitative, not decorative. Uttermost never means very. It means as far as the thing can go, which is precisely why Hebrews 7:25 uses it of salvation and not of sentiment.
scriptures: Hebrews 7:25
Wherefore he is able also to save them to the uttermost that come unto God by him, seeing he ever liveth to make intercession for them.
Psalm 2:8
Ask of me, and I shall give thee the heathen for thine inheritance, and the uttermost parts of the earth for thy possession.
Acts 1:8

But ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you: and ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth.
1 Thessalonians 2:16
Forbidding us to speak to the Gentiles that they might be saved, to fill up their sins alway: for the wrath is come upon them to the uttermost.
corruption_summary: Uttermost is corrupted when Hebrews 7:25 is read as an offer of salvation’s availability rather than a statement of its completeness — making Christ able to save anyone partway rather than able to save His own the whole way.
corruption_paragraphs: The common evangelical reduction turns able to save to the uttermost into able to save even the worst sinner. That is true, but it is not what the verse says, and the substitution costs the reader the doctrine. The adverb does not modify the sinner’s badness; it modifies the salvation’s extent. Christ saves completely, finally, to the end. Read the second half of the verse and the point is unmistakable: the reason He saves to the uttermost is that He ever liveth to make intercession. The permanence of the priesthood is the ground of the permanence of the salvation. Strip out the adverb’s real force and Hebrews 7 stops being an argument about the superiority of Melchizedek’s order and becomes a bare invitation.

The second corruption runs the other direction. Where uttermost is used of wrath — the wrath is come upon them to the uttermost (1 Thessalonians 2:16) — the modern instinct is to soften it into a temporary corrective, a chastening that must eventually exhaust itself. That is Origen’s error revived, and every historic Christian confession rejects it. The same word that measures the completeness of salvation measures the completeness of judgment. A reader who wants the full comfort of Hebrews 7:25 must accept that the Authorized Version means the whole distance in both directions.
roots_summary: Two Greek words and two Hebrew words carry uttermost in the Authorized Version, and they divide cleanly between degree and distance. The degree words stand behind the doctrine of perseverance; the distance words stand behind the Great Commission.
roots_lines: Greek pantelēs (G3838) — complete, perfect, to the very end (Hebrews 7:25, save them to the uttermost). Degree, not distance.
Greek eschatos (G2078) — last, farthest, extreme (Acts 1:8, the uttermost part of the earth). Distance, not degree.
Greek telos (G5056) — end, completion, the appointed finish (1 Thessalonians 2:16, to the uttermost, of wrath run out to its term).
Hebrew ephes (H657) — end, extremity, the place where there is nothing further (Psalm 2:8, the uttermost parts of the earth).
usage: Christ saves to the uttermost because He ever liveth (Hebrews 7:25) — the permanence of the Priest is the ground of the permanence of the salvation.
The Father’s promise to the Son reaches the uttermost parts of the earth (Psalm 2:8); the Son’s commission to the church reaches the same edge (Acts 1:8).
Wrath also has an uttermost (1 Thessalonians 2:16). The word measures the whole distance in both directions, or it measures nothing.

etymology: Past tense and participle of rend: Old English rendan, to tear, to cut down. Webster 1828 gives RENT as the past of rend and as a noun, a fissure, a break, a schism. In the Authorized Version the word is almost always violent and almost always public — garments torn in grief, a mantle torn as a sign, a veil torn from the top.
biblical_def: To be rent in Scripture is to be torn open, and the tearing nearly always says something the mouth has not yet said. Jacob, shown the bloodied coat, rent his clothes, and put sackcloth upon his loins, and mourned for his son many days (Genesis 37:34). Samuel’s mantle tears in Saul’s hand and the tear itself becomes the oracle: as Samuel turned about to go away, he laid hold upon the skirt of his mantle, and it rent (1 Samuel 15:27). Rending garments was the ancient body’s confession that something had broken which could not be mended by tidiness. Which is exactly why Joel turns the word inward: And rend your heart, and not your garments, and turn unto the LORD your God (Joel 2:13). The outward tear is cheap; God asks for the inward one. Then the Authorized Version puts the word where it truly belongs. At the death of Christ, the veil of the temple was rent in twain from the top to the bottom (Matthew 27:51). Man rends from the collar down. This tear began at the top, because God tore it. Every earlier rending in Scripture was a creature grieving over a barrier; this one was the Creator abolishing it.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 gives RENT as the past tense and participle of rend, to tear, and as a noun: a fissure, a break, a laceration; also a schism, a breach of union, as a rent in a church.
webster_full: RENT, pp. of rend — Torn asunder; split or burst by violence. RENT, n. — A fissure; a break; a laceration; a place torn. Also, a schism; a breach of union.

Webster’s second sense is the theological one. A rent is not damage merely; it is a division that shows. The word travels from cloth to congregation without changing meaning, which is why the Authorized Version can use it of a coat, a mantle, and a temple curtain and mean the same violent honesty each time.
scriptures: Matthew 27:51
And, behold, the veil of the temple was rent in twain from the top to the bottom; and the earth did quake, and the rocks rent;
Genesis 37:34
And Jacob rent his clothes, and put sackcloth upon his loins, and mourned for his son many days.
Joel 2:13
And rend your heart, and not your garments, and turn unto the LORD your God: for he is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness, and repenteth him of the evil.
1 Samuel 15:27
And as Samuel turned about to go away, he laid hold upon the skirt of his mantle, and it rent.
corruption_summary: Rent is corrupted when the torn veil of Matthew 27:51 is reduced to a symbol of general spiritual openness rather than the abolition of a specific barrier by a specific sacrifice, and when Joel’s rend your heart is softened from repentance into sincerity.
corruption_paragraphs: The torn veil is regularly preached as though it announced that God is now approachable in general — the end of formality, the beginning of intimacy. That is a thin reading of a violent verse. The veil was a working piece of architecture that kept sinners out of the holy of holies on pain of death, and it was rent from the top to the bottom, which is the narrator’s way of naming the hand that did it. The barrier did not relax; it was destroyed, and it was destroyed at the moment the Substitute died. Hebrews draws the line the text intends: the new and living way is through the veil, that is to say, his flesh. Access is not a mood God came into. It is a purchase Christ made.

Joel 2:13 suffers a quieter corruption. Rend your heart, and not your garments is read as a warning against ritualism and then domesticated into a call for authenticity — be genuine, do not merely go through the motions. But Joel is not contrasting the fake with the sincere; he is contrasting the cheap with the costly. Rending a garment took a second and a seam. Rending the heart is repentance, and repentance is the death of self-defence. The prophet then names the only reason a man would dare it: for he is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness. Sincerity is not the ground of that appeal. The character of God is.
roots_summary: The Hebrew and Greek behind rent are ordinary words for tearing, deliberately kept ordinary. Scripture does not reach for a special vocabulary at the veil; it uses the same verb a man uses for his shirt, and lets the object carry the weight.
roots_lines: Hebrew qāra’ — to tear, to rend (Genesis 37:34; 1 Samuel 15:27; Joel 2:13). Untagged in this lexicon; no Strong’s page is minted for it here.
Greek schizō — to split, to cleave apart (Matthew 27:51, rent in twain). The English schism descends from it, which is Webster’s second sense exactly.
Greek diarrēssō (G1284) — to tear asunder, to rend, used of the high priest rending his clothes at the trial of Christ.
Hebrew bāqa‘ (H1234) — to cleave, to split, to break through; the harder cousin of rending, used of the earth and the sea.
usage: Jacob rent his clothes (Genesis 37:34) — grief in the ancient world was worn, not managed.
Joel moves the verb inward: rend your heart, and not your garments (Joel 2:13). The garment costs a seam; the heart costs the self.
The veil was rent in twain from the top to the bottom (Matthew 27:51). Man tears downward. That tear started where God is.

etymology: Past tense of pitch, Middle English picchen, to thrust in, to fix, to set firmly. Webster 1828: to throw or thrust; to fix; to set in array; to fix a tent or temporary habitation. In the Authorized Version the word belongs almost entirely to tents — and therefore to the whole doctrine of dwelling, from Abram’s canvas to the true tabernacle which the Lord pitched.
biblical_def: Pitched is a tent word, and in Scripture tents are never merely shelter; they are a confession about where a man belongs. Abram and Lot part, and the narrator marks the difference in one clause: Abram dwelled in the land of Canaan, and Lot dwelled in the cities of the plain, and pitched his tent toward Sodom (Genesis 13:12). Nobody pitches a tent by accident. The direction of the door is the direction of the heart, and Lot’s door faced the city he would eventually have to be dragged out of. Jacob, returning, pitched his tent before the city of Shechem (Genesis 33:18). Moses took the tabernacle, and pitched it without the camp, afar off from the camp (Exodus 33:7) — a pitching that was itself a judgment, putting the meeting place outside a people who had just made a calf. Then Hebrews takes the humble verb and gives it to God: Christ is a minister of the sanctuary, and of the true tabernacle, which the Lord pitched, and not man (Hebrews 8:2). Every tent Israel ever staked was a copy. The original was pitched by God, and John says the Word did the same thing in flesh when He dwelt — tabernacled — among us.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines PITCH as a verb: to throw or thrust; to fix or plant; to set in order or array; and specifically, to fix or set a tent, to encamp. PITCHED is its past tense and participle: fixed, planted, set in array, encamped.
webster_full: PITCH, v.t. — To throw or thrust; to fix or plant; to set, as a tent or temporary habitation; to set in array; to regulate or set, as a tune. PITCHED, pp. — Set; planted; fixed; encamped; set in order.

Webster’s first sense is force and his second is permanence, and the Authorized Version needs both. A tent is pitched by driving something into the ground. The paradox of the patriarchs is that the most portable dwelling in the ancient world is fixed by an act of hammering — which is exactly the life of faith Hebrews 11 describes: staked down hard, and still not home.
scriptures: Hebrews 8:2
A minister of the sanctuary, and of the true tabernacle, which the Lord pitched, and not man.
Genesis 13:12
Abram dwelled in the land of Canaan, and Lot dwelled in the cities of the plain, and pitched his tent toward Sodom.
Exodus 33:7

And Moses took the tabernacle, and pitched it without the camp, afar off from the camp, and called it the Tabernacle of the congregation. And it came to pass, that every one which sought the LORD went out unto the tabernacle of the congregation, which was without the camp.
Genesis 33:18
And Jacob came to Shalem, a city of Shechem, which is in the land of Canaan, when he came from Padanaram; and pitched his tent before the city.
corruption_summary: Pitched is corrupted when the patriarchal tent is romanticized into a picture of spiritual freedom from commitment, and when Hebrews 8:2 — the tabernacle which the Lord pitched, and not man — is read as a metaphor rather than as the argument for the obsolescence of the whole earthly sanctuary system.
corruption_paragraphs: There is a familiar devotional use of the patriarchs’ tents that turns them into a warrant for rootlessness — travel light, hold nothing, keep your options open. Scripture’s point is nearly the opposite. Abraham was not uncommitted; he was committed to a city he could not yet see, and the tent was the cost of that commitment, not its reward. Hebrews 11 says plainly that he looked for a city which hath foundations, whose builder and maker is God. The tent testifies to a settled hope, not a loose grip. Lot proves the point negatively: he is the one who kept his options open, pitched toward Sodom, and ended up with neither the tent nor the city.

The heavier misreading falls on Hebrews 8:2. When the true tabernacle, which the Lord pitched, and not man is taken as poetic language for God’s nearness, the letter’s central argument is lost. The writer is making a structural claim: the earthly sanctuary was a copy and shadow, and the arrival of the real one renders the copy finished. That is why he can say the first covenant is decaying and ready to vanish away. Any theology that keeps a standing earthly priesthood, a repeated propitiatory sacrifice, or a mediating altar has not reckoned with the verb. The Lord pitched the true tabernacle. Man’s pitching is over.
roots_summary: Three Hebrew verbs and one Greek verb stand behind pitched. The Hebrew divides between stretching a tent out, dwelling in one, and encamping with a company — and the Greek word for the tabernacle God pitched is the ordinary word for driving a stake.
roots_lines: Hebrew nātāh (H5186) — to stretch out, to extend, to spread a tent (Exodus 33:7, Moses pitched it without the camp).
Hebrew āhal (H167) — to pitch a tent, to move a tent, to dwell in tents (Genesis 13:12, Lot pitched his tent toward Sodom).
Hebrew chānāh (H2583) — to encamp, to pitch camp as a company (Genesis 33:18, Jacob before Shechem).
Greek pēgnumi (G4078) — to fix, to fasten, to pitch (Hebrews 8:2, the true tabernacle, which the Lord pitched).
usage: Pitched his tent toward Sodom (Genesis 13:12) — the direction of the door is the direction of the heart.
Moses pitched the tabernacle outside the camp (Exodus 33:7); the location of the meeting place was itself a verdict on the camp.
The true tabernacle is the one which the Lord pitched, and not man (Hebrews 8:2) — every stake Israel drove was a copy of it.

etymology: Old English betera, the comparative of gōd (good), from a root meaning to remedy or make good. Webster 1828: having good qualities in a greater degree than another; improved in health; more advantageous. In the Authorized Version better is the load-bearing word of the epistle to the Hebrews, where it is used thirteen times to argue that what Christ brought does not supplement the old covenant but supersedes it.
biblical_def: Better is a comparative, and comparatives are arguments. The writer to the Hebrews builds his entire case on this one word: Jesus is made a surety of a better testament (Hebrews 7:22); He is the mediator of a better covenant, which was established upon better promises (Hebrews 8:6); the patriarchs desire a better country, that is, an heavenly (Hebrews 11:16). The Greek behind it, kreittōn, means stronger, more excellent, of higher rank — not merely more pleasant. That distinction is the whole argument. The old covenant was not bad; it was God-given, holy, just and good. It was simply weaker, because it ran through dying priests, repeated blood, and a copy of a sanctuary. What is better is better in the way a substance is better than its shadow. The word is not confined to Hebrews. David measures a single day against a thousand: a day in thy courts is better than a thousand (Psalm 84:10). Paul weighs his own death against continued usefulness and finds to be with Christ; which is far better (Philippians 1:23). In every case the comparison is not sentimental preference. It is a valuation, and the believer is expected to make it soberly and then act on it.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines BETTER as having good qualities in a greater degree than another; superior in excellence, worth, usefulness or acceptableness; improved in health; more advantageous. Webster notes it is the comparative of good, supplied from a different root.
webster_full: BETTER, a. [comparative of good, supplied from a different root.] — Having good qualities in a greater degree than another; superior in excellence, worth, usefulness or acceptableness. Improved in health; less sick than before. More advantageous.

Webster’s phrase superior in excellence, worth, usefulness is precisely the register of Hebrews. The letter never says the old covenant was worthless; it says the new one is of higher worth. A comparison is only meaningful when both terms are real, which is why the argument requires the reader to honour Moses before he can measure Christ against him.
scriptures: Hebrews 7:22
By so much was Jesus made a surety of a better testament.
Hebrews 8:6
But now hath he obtained a more excellent ministry, by how much also he is the mediator of a better covenant, which was established upon better promises.
Hebrews 11:16
But now they desire a better country, that is, an heavenly: wherefore God is not ashamed to be called their God: for he hath prepared for them a city.
Psalm 84:10
For a day in thy courts is better than a thousand. I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God, than to dwell in the tents of wickedness.
Philippians 1:23
For I am in a strait betwixt two, having a desire to depart, and to be with Christ; which is far better:
corruption_summary: Better is corrupted when the comparative of Hebrews is flattened into a claim that the old covenant was defective or sub-Christian, and equally when it is softened into mere preference — two errors that between them dissolve either the unity of Scripture or the finality of Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: The older error runs toward Marcion and never entirely dies: if the new covenant is better, the old must have been bad, its God harsher, its law an obstacle. Hebrews forbids this. The law was given by God, the tabernacle was patterned by God, the priesthood was appointed by God, and the writer treats every one of them with reverence. His argument is that a shadow is genuinely cast by a genuine body. What made the first covenant weak was not its author but its instruments — priests who died, blood that could not cleanse the conscience, a sanctuary made with hands. The Reformed reading holds both covenants as administrations of one covenant of grace, and it is precisely that unity which makes better intelligible rather than insulting.

The modern error is smaller and more common: better becomes a word of taste. Philippians 1:23 gets read as Paul expressing a personal preference for heaven, and Psalm 84:10 as poetic enthusiasm for church attendance. But Paul is doing arithmetic under the shadow of a possible execution, and David is stating a ratio — one day against a thousand, a doorkeeper’s post against the tents of wickedness. Scripture’s comparatives are valuations a man is expected to act upon. When better means only what I happen to like more, the entire logic of counting the cost collapses, and with it the possibility of martyrdom, which is simply this word taken seriously.
roots_summary: The Authorized Version’s better renders a Greek comparative of strength and rank in Hebrews, and the ordinary Hebrew word for good in comparative constructions in the Old Testament. The difference matters: the Hebrew compares goods, the Greek compares ranks.
roots_lines: Greek kreittōn — stronger, more excellent, of higher rank; the structural word of Hebrews (7:22; 8:6; 11:16). Untagged in this lexicon; no Strong’s page is minted for it here.
Hebrew tōv (H2896) — good, pleasant, beneficial; rendered better in comparative constructions (Psalm 84:10, better than a thousand).
Greek hyperechō (G5242) — to surpass, to excel, to be superior; the cousin idea behind a more excellent ministry (Hebrews 8:6).
Greek para (G3844) — beside, alongside; the preposition Hebrews uses to set the two covenants side by side so the comparison can be made at all.
usage: Hebrews argues by comparative: a better testament, a better covenant, better promises, a better country — superiority of rank, not a correction of a mistake.
A day in thy courts is better than a thousand (Psalm 84:10) is a ratio, not a compliment.
To be with Christ; which is far better (Philippians 1:23) — Paul weighs death against usefulness and reports the sum.

etymology: From Old English an (one) and other. Webster 1828: not the same; different; one more, in addition. The English word hides a distinction the Greek New Testament makes plainly — between allos, another of the same kind, and heteros, another of a different kind — and Galatians 1 turns on it.
biblical_def: Another looks like the plainest word in the Bible, and it carries one of its sharpest edges. Paul writes to a church drifting toward a rival message: I marvel that ye are so soon removed from him that called you into the grace of Christ unto another gospel: Which is not another (Galatians 1:6-7). In English that reads like a contradiction. In Greek it is exact. The first another is heteros, a different kind of thing; the second is allos, another of the same kind. Paul is saying: they are peddling a gospel of a different kind, which is not a second gospel at all, because there is only one. A rival gospel is not an alternative; it is a counterfeit. The same distinction blesses in the other direction. Christ promises, I will pray the Father, and he shall give you another Comforter (John 14:16) — allos, another of the same kind. The Spirit is not a lesser substitute for the departing Son but a Comforter of the same divine order, which is a plain testimony to His deity. And Paul warns the Corinthians against another Jesus, another spirit, another gospel (2 Corinthians 11:4). The whole doctrine of the exclusivity of Christ sits inside this small word.
webster_summary: Webster 1828 defines ANOTHER as not the same; different: as, we have another task to perform. Also, one more, in addition to a former number; and any other, any different person indefinitely.
webster_full: ANOTHER, a. [of an or one, and other.] — Not the same; different; as, we have one form of government; France has another. One more, in addition to a former number. Any other; any different person, indefinitely.

Webster’s first two senses are exactly the Greek pair. Not the same; different is heteros. One more, in addition to a former number is allos. English collapses them into one spelling; the New Testament keeps them apart, and Galatians 1:6-7 is unreadable until the reader knows it.
scriptures: Galatians 1:6
I marvel that ye are so soon removed from him that called you into the grace of Christ unto another gospel:
Galatians 1:7
Which is not another; but there be some that trouble you, and would pervert the gospel of Christ.
John 14:16
And I will pray the Father, and he shall give you another Comforter, that he may abide with you for ever;
2 Corinthians 11:4

For if he that cometh preacheth another Jesus, whom we have not preached, or if ye receive another spirit, which ye have not received, or another gospel, which ye have not accepted, ye might well bear with him.
Isaiah 42:8
I am the LORD: that is my name: and my glory will I not give to another, neither my praise to graven images.
corruption_summary: Another is corrupted when Galatians 1 is read as Paul objecting to a rival denomination rather than denying that a rival gospel exists at all, and when John 14:16 is used to make the Spirit a substitute for Christ rather than a Comforter of the same divine kind.
corruption_paragraphs: The pressure on Galatians 1 is always toward pluralism: Paul had his emphasis, the Judaizers had theirs, and the modern reader is invited to regret the heat of the exchange. The grammar refuses this. Paul does not say the other message is a worse gospel or an incomplete gospel; he says it is not another — there is no second item in the category. He then pronounces an anathema twice, which is not the language of a man adjudicating between traditions. Any framework that treats justification by faith alone as one legitimate reading among several has already conceded what Paul spent the letter denying. A gospel that adds a work of the law to the finished work of Christ is not a variant of Christianity. It is its rival.

The corruption at John 14:16 is quieter and more devotional. Another Comforter is often preached as though the Spirit were sent to fill the gap left by an absent Christ — a stand-in for the real thing. But allos means another of the same kind, and the whole point is that nothing is lost in the exchange: the disciples do not trade a divine Person for a lesser influence. This is one of the clearest incidental proofs of the Spirit’s full deity in the Gospels, and treating Him as a substitute quietly demotes the third Person of the Trinity to an instrument. He is not Christ’s replacement; He is Christ’s own promise, of the same rank, given to abide for ever.
roots_summary: Two Greek adjectives lie under the single English word, and the New Testament uses the difference deliberately. Where the Authorized Version prints another twice in one sentence, as in Galatians 1:6-7, the reader should assume the Greek has switched words on purpose.
roots_lines: Greek allos (G243) — another of the same kind, one more of the same sort (John 14:16, another Comforter; Galatians 1:7, which is not another).
Greek heteros (G2087) — another of a different kind, a different sort altogether (Galatians 1:6, another gospel; the word behind English heterodox).
Greek euangelion (G2098) — gospel, good news; the noun both adjectives modify in Galatians 1, and the reason the distinction is not academic.
Hebrew achēr — another, other, strange; the word behind the other gods of the first commandment and behind Isaiah 42:8, my glory will I not give to another. Untagged in this lexicon.
usage: Another gospel: which is not another (Galatians 1:6-7) — a different kind of message, and therefore not a second gospel at all.
Another Comforter (John 14:16) is allos: the Spirit is of the same divine kind as the Son, not a lesser stand-in.
Another Jesus, another spirit, another gospel (2 Corinthians 11:4) — counterfeits travel together, and they travel in threes.
